questions.q: Why does LTV Global reject point-to-point integration between its major systems?
options: Because point-to-point integration is always slower at runtime than hub-based integration
Because it doesn't scale past the first few integrations, creates no reusable logic, and makes integration knowledge a single developer's tribal dependency
Because Salesforce technically prohibits direct callouts to external systems
Because point-to-point integration cannot use REST APIs
questions.explain: The lesson's core argument against point-to-point is scale and maintainability: each new system multiplies direct connections with no reuse, and knowledge gets trapped with whoever built each specific connection.

questions.q: Which Enterprise Integration Pattern does this lesson use for deciding whether a Parts Order needs manual credit review before proceeding?
options: Message Router
Message Translator
Content-Based Router
Aggregator
questions.explain: A Content-Based Router inspects the actual content of a Parts Order to decide its path (manual credit review vs. straight through) — a specialized router making decisions based on what's inside the message, not just its type or origin.

questions.q: What integration style does LTV Global use for LedgerPoint, and why?
options: Synchronous REST callouts, because LedgerPoint has a modern API
Platform Events only, because LedgerPoint supports event-driven publishing
Batch-only, nightly SFTP flat files in both directions, because LedgerPoint has no API of any kind
No integration at all — LedgerPoint is excluded from this design
questions.explain: LedgerPoint has no API, so batch SFTP flat files are the only viable mechanism — a permanent constraint from Lesson 4, not a temporary gap, and Lesson 14 details this integration fully.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say different systems in LTV Global's landscape use different integration styles rather than one uniform mechanism?
options: Because using a single mechanism everywhere is against Salesforce policy
Because each system's integration style reflects what that specific system can actually support, per Lesson 4's current-state constraints
Because different regions require legally different integration mechanisms
Because batch integration is always preferred over real-time regardless of system capability
questions.explain: The matching of style to system (synchronous for Meridian orders, batch for LedgerPoint and Snowflake, event-driven for downstream fan-out) directly reflects each system's real capabilities established in the current-state analysis, not an arbitrary uniform policy.

questions.q: In the Lab scenario, what is the risk of allowing a 'just this once' direct Apex callout from Salesforce straight to Meridian, bypassing the integration hub?
options: There is no risk; it is actually the recommended approach for all integrations
It begins the exact point-to-point sprawl the hub decision was designed to avoid, undermining the shared, documented, reusable integration layer
It would violate Meridian's SOAP-only API requirement
It would require disabling Change Data Capture platform-wide
questions.explain: Allowing exceptions for convenience is exactly how point-to-point integration re-emerges even after a hub decision is made — each 'just this once' connection erodes the reuse and maintainability the hub exists to provide.
